source: Gero (1990) Design prototypes: a knowledge representation schema for design (AI Magazine 11(4):26-36)
finding: Founding paper of FBS. A design prototype stores function, behaviour, structure and knowledge in one schema. Designing is modelled as eight processes between F, Be, Bs, S and design description D.
numbers: Eight processes: formulation, synthesis, analysis, evaluation, documentation, reformulation 1 (structure), 2 (behaviour), 3 (function). Source could not be fetched (403); details taken from secondary papers a02-a04.
limits: Not opened. Described via Gero, Kan & Pourmohamadi 2011 and Kannengiesser & Zhu 2009 which I did read.
agent_relevance: Gives the schema a ready 6-variable state vocabulary (F, Be, Bs, S, D plus requirements R) and a small named set of transitions between them.

source: Gero, Kan & Pourmohamadi (2011) Analysing design protocols: development of methods and tools
finding: FBS ontology as a coding scheme. Goal of designing = turn functions into design descriptions through a series of transformations, never directly. Requirements R come from the client and are outside the designer's control.
numbers: Variables: R, F, Be, Bs, S, D. Eight processes: formulation (F to Be, process 1), synthesis (Be to S, 2), analysis (S to Bs, 3), evaluation (Be vs Bs, 4), documentation (S to D, 5), reformulation I/II/III (structure, behaviour, function; 6-8).
quote: A design description is never transformed directly from the function but is a result of a series of processes among the FBS variables.
limits: A coding scheme, not a performance theory. It says what moves occur, not which order is best. Authors note it is one of several possible general schemes.
agent_relevance: A map for an agent: function to expected behaviour to structure to derived behaviour to a compare step. Candidate for S-states: spec, expected-behaviour list, candidate, derived-behaviour, compare.

source: Kannengiesser & Zhu (2009) An ontologically-based evaluation of software design methods
finding: Situated FBS (Gero & Kannengiesser 2004) adds three worlds (external, interpreted, expected) and 20 processes. The 20 processes map onto 8 fundamental design steps. Reformulations break any linear waterfall order.
numbers: 20 processes; 8 steps; 3 reformulation types. Formulation builds a state space of expected F, B, S. Synthesis picks a structure from that space. Analysis derives behaviour. Evaluation compares expected and derived behaviour (process 15).
quote: The three types of reformulation provide the potential to break this sequence.
limits: Framework is stated in text and diagrams. It is a conceptual model; the paper gives no empirical test of the 20 processes themselves.
agent_relevance: Reformulation = changing which F, B or S we focus on. This lines up with our reframe operator: it should fire after a failed compare, not on a clock (G1).

source: Kannengiesser & Zhu (2009) An ontologically-based evaluation of software design methods
finding: Push-pull idea: interpretation and constructive memory are driven both by the stored experience (push) and the current expectations (pull). Same input can be seen differently at different times.
numbers: Cites Suwa et al. 1999: unexpected discoveries in sketches correlate with new requirements. Cites Guindon 1990: protocols of software designers show frequent discovery of new requirements mixed with partial solutions.
quote: designers try to make the most effective use of newly inferred requirements, or the sudden discovery of partial solutions
limits: Secondary citations; the underlying studies were not opened here.
agent_relevance: Supports allowing requirement revision mid-run when real output exposes a new need (G2), instead of freezing the first problem statement.

source: Kannengiesser & Zhu (2009) An ontologically-based evaluation of software design methods
finding: FBS applied to design methods as artefacts. Evaluated five software design methods (ADD, S4V, RUP, BAPO, Agile Alliance Approach) by which of the 20 processes each supports and how (implicit, managerial, procedural).
numbers: 5 methods x 20 processes. Interpretation and constructive memory are supported only by lightweight (implicit) approaches in most methods. Re-interpretation to produce new concepts is supported only by AAA. Focussing on F, B and S is supported by ADD, S4V and RUP; BAPO only F; AAA only F and B.
limits: Qualitative mapping by two authors from method text; no inter-rater check reported. RUP analysed only from an introductory description.
agent_relevance: Most methods cover synthesis and analysis but leave reinterpretation and reformulation implicit. Our schema should make reformulation explicit and code-triggered.

source: Gero, Kan & Pourmohamadi (2011) Analysing design protocols: development of methods and tools
finding: Protocol measurement toolkit built on the FBS code. One segment gets one code. Transitions between segments define processes: syntactic (adjacent segments) or semantic (linkograph backlinks).
numbers: Example: originating segment S backlinked to Be gives process Be to S = synthesis. Demo protocol: large industry team, over 1 hour, 1280 segments. Tool LINKOgrapher gives tabular stats, dynamic issues, dynamic processes, dynamic entropy, first-order and second-order Markov, first passage.
limits: Syntactic version is called a weak model of design processes by the authors. Coding reliability numbers not given in this paper.
agent_relevance: Gives ready metrics for tracing an LLM run: issue mix, transition matrix, first-passage time per issue (how fast it returns to the same issue).

source: Gero, Kan & Pourmohamadi (2011) Analysing design protocols: development of methods and tools
finding: Markov and entropy models. First-order Markov: probability that one issue follows another. Second-order: probability of an issue following a process (8 rows by 6 columns). First passage: mean segments before returning to the same issue (focus). Entropy of linkographs linked to productivity.
numbers: Window size used in demo: 1/10 of protocol length. Prior use of Markov models showed a lack of evaluation (process 4) in 3D virtual world design sessions. Entropy used to study fixation and commitment.
limits: Entropy-productivity link is an argument (Kan & Gero) not tested here; no effect size given.
agent_relevance: Cheap code-side diagnostics for impasse and fixation: low entropy plus long first-passage on S could flag a stuck loop. Hypothesis only.

source: Gero, Kan & Pourmohamadi (2011) Analysing design protocols: development of methods and tools
finding: Cross-domain comparison made possible by the common code: architects versus software designers coded with the same scheme, issue distributions and Markov process models compared.
numbers: Result figures only (Figs 7-8); no numbers in text. Claim: protocols from individual, team, student, professional and remote designers all fit the same scheme.
limits: Illustrative examples, not a hypothesis test. Numbers not extractable from the text.
agent_relevance: Weak support for domain independence of the state set; do not over-claim.

source: Gero & Milovanovic (2020) A framework for studying design thinking through measuring designers' minds, bodies and brains
finding: Review of design cognition measurement. FBS is the most widely used coding ontology in design protocol research. Used in architecture, engineering, software and systems design, including over 10,000 hours of industry design coded.
numbers: Two FBS papers (Gero 1990; Gero & Kannengiesser 2004) had over 3,500 citations between them (Google Scholar, 15 Jan 2020). Contrast: over 900 in 2011 (Gero, Kan & Pourmohamadi).
limits: Citation counts show use, not validity. Review author is the framework's own originator, so there is self-citation bias.
agent_relevance: Popularity as a coding scheme means a lot of labelled human design data exists, which could be used to calibrate any LLM FBS tagger.

source: Gero & Milovanovic (2020) A framework for studying design thinking through measuring designers' minds, bodies and brains
finding: Meta-coding of FBS: requirement, function and expected behaviour are problem-space issues; structure and structure-behaviour are solution-space issues. Plot of problem vs solution issues over time shows problem-solution co-evolution (Maher & Poon 1996; Dorst & Cross 2001; Jiang, Gero & Yen 2014).
numbers: FBS grouped into 2 meta-codes: problem = R, F, Be; solution = S, Bs. Second-order code adding 'new' and 'surprising' issues used to model creativity trend (Gero & Kan 2016).
limits: Maher & Poon is cited here, original not opened. This is the link to Maher in this subfield: co-evolution of problem and solution spaces.
agent_relevance: A simple two-bucket monitor for our agent: ratio of problem-side to solution-side moves per window, with a flag if one side never changes after the first draft.

source: Gero & Milovanovic (2020) A framework for studying design thinking through measuring designers' minds, bodies and brains
finding: Kannengiesser & Gero (2019) used FBS protocols to ask if designers think fast or slow. All student and professional designers across several protocol studies show both System 1 and System 2 patterns. Song (2017) found expertise-linked differences in effort on decomposing and recomposing problems (freshmen, seniors, professionals).
numbers: No sample sizes or percentages given in the review text.
limits: Reported second-hand; the 2019 paper itself not opened.
agent_relevance: Both fast routine moves and slow reasoning appear in the same designer. Supports mixing cheap pass-through steps with checked steps, not one fixed depth.

source: Kannengiesser & Gero (draft, c.2015) Is designing independent of domain? Comparing models of engineering, software and service design
finding: Quantitative simulation of three published design process models by mapping their steps onto the 20 sFBS processes. Compared Pahl and Beitz (engineering), RUP (software) and DFSS-ICOV (service).
numbers: Steps coded: Pahl-Beitz 29 activities (87 mappings), RUP 35 activities (100 mappings), DFSS-ICOV 7 activities (41 mappings). Iteration scenarios S1/S2/S3 give 154/235/302 steps (Pahl-Beitz), 185/278/363 (RUP), 70/103/132 (DFSS-ICOV).
limits: A simulation from model text, not from observed designers. Authors assume each step happens once per iteration, which they admit is unrealistic. Draft version.
agent_relevance: Shows that a process spec can be turned into a sequence of FBS issues and checked against a profile. Same trick could audit our own schema's flow.

source: Kannengiesser & Gero (draft, c.2015) Is designing independent of domain? Comparing models of engineering, software and service design
finding: All three engineering, software and service models share four phases (clarify problem, concept structure, solution structure, deliver). In the simulation, R, F, Be and D occur at the start; S and Bs occur later. Structure and description issues grow linearly.
numbers: Pattern held in all three models and all three scenarios. Cumulative-occurrence measures: slope, first occurrence at start, continuity, linearity (R2 >= 0.95). Only function issues shared a common slope across the models: F(2,5)=5.224, p=0.06. Other issues differ: Be F(2,5)=101.5, Bs F(2,4)=319.3, S F(2,6)=11.9, D F(2,6)=220.8, all p<0.05.
limits: Common slope for function is not significant at 0.05 (p=0.06). Tiny n (a handful of slopes per issue). Domain independence is only weakly supported: the commonalities are mostly about ordering, not rates.
agent_relevance: A fair statement: phase order looks shared across domains; rates are not. Do not hard-code issue ratios.

source: Kannengiesser & Gero (draft, c.2015) Is designing independent of domain? Comparing models of engineering, software and service design
finding: Structure-behaviour (Bs) rate differs strongly between models. Bs slope: Pahl-Beitz 0.065 vs RUP about 0.12. Structure slope about 0.42 (Pahl-Beitz) vs 0.39 (RUP) vs 0.34-0.38 (DFSS). Description slope 0.19-0.20 (Pahl-Beitz), 0.24-0.25 (RUP), 0.32-0.34 (DFSS).
numbers: Bs slope: Pahl-Beitz 0.065 (R2 0.96-0.99) vs RUP 0.120-0.127 (R2 0.97-0.98). Expected behaviour slope: 0.207-0.217 (Pahl-Beitz) vs 0.153-0.157 (RUP). R2 for S in RUP up to 0.999.
limits: Values are from simulations of prescribed methods, not people. Pahl-Beitz checks derived behaviour about half as often as RUP.
agent_relevance: Software-style processes check derived behaviour about twice as often as classic engineering stage-gate. Hints that tasks with cheap code-run evaluation should evaluate more often.

source: Design Science paper: Can Pahl and Beitz' systematic approach be a predictive model of designing?
finding: Test of whether Pahl and Beitz's Systematic Approach predicts real student designing. 46 sessions coded with FBS. Predicts most behaviour but fails on early structure and structure-behaviour.
numbers: Study 1: 15 sessions, pairs of 2nd-year mechanical engineering students, 45 min each. Study 2: 31 sessions of senior capstone pairs (brainstorming 10, morphological analysis 11, TRIZ 10). 4 assistive-technology briefs. Two independent coders. Model: 87 steps, 235 steps with iterations. Agreement threshold 85% across sessions.
limits: Descriptive only: no inferential tests in the text I could read; table values were images. Students, short sessions, small n per condition (10-15). Key deviation: Bs and S appear early in students but the model predicts later. Year of paper not confirmed (about 2018).
agent_relevance: A real-data failure of a waterfall FBS flow. Students jump to a structure early and reason about it. An agent that waits for a full spec before proposing a candidate may deviate from how good human reasoning works (needs testing, not assuming).

source: Design Science paper: Can Pahl and Beitz' systematic approach be a predictive model of designing?
finding: Continuity and linearity patterns: Bs, S and D continuous in students and the model; R, F, Be discontinuous. Bs and S linear, F and Be nonlinear in both. Bs slope much lower in the model than in the data; S slope similar.
numbers: In 3 concept-generation datasets: Bs and S linear in all, F and Be nonlinear in all, D linear except TRIZ; R had under 10 occurrences so no analysis. Bs slope clearly lower in the model than in the empirical data.
limits: Exact slope and R2 values not recoverable from text. No multiple-testing control, no CIs.
agent_relevance: Humans produce structure-behaviour checks more often than the textbook method predicts. Supports more frequent code-run checks.

source: Ralph (2013) Software engineering process theory: a multi-method comparison of Sensemaking-Coevolution-Implementation theory and Function-Behavior-Structure theory
finding: Field test of FBS against a rival process theory (Sensemaking-Coevolution-Implementation, SCI) in software development. SCI beat FBS on the survey and on four case studies. FBS says goals are given and phases are ordered; SCI says goals co-evolve with the design.
numbers: Survey: 1384 completers from 65 countries (of 4410 visitors, 31%), 13 contrast items. Negative skew toward SCI significant for every item (chi-square p<0.001). 96.6% of respondents had a median response agreeing or strongly agreeing with SCI. H1 (SCI better) supported; H2 (FBS better) not supported. 4 case studies; FBS propositions 1-4 (formulation, synthesis, analysis/evaluation, weak coupling of framing and design) not supported in the cases.
limits: Self-report survey with forced-contrast items; the SCI pole may read as the socially preferred answer. FBS tested as if prescriptive, though it is mainly an ontology. Case sizes small (5, 5, 25-100, 7 participants). No effect size.
agent_relevance: Strongest published challenge to a linear F-to-B-to-S process. Argues for a loop with problem reframing, as in our schema, rather than a one-way pipe. Does not refute FBS as a coding scheme.

source: Ralph (2013) Software engineering process theory: a multi-method comparison of Sensemaking-Coevolution-Implementation theory and Function-Behavior-Structure theory
finding: Case-level detail: FBS formulation step (deriving expected behaviour from function) was not seen because goal statements were vague. Synthesis was not seen as a clean step. No evidence of behaviour prediction before building.
numbers: Cases: C1 Canada Scrum e-business, C2 UK ad hoc e-commerce, C3 UK education PRINCE2, C4 UK education Scrum-like. Teams of 5 to 100.
limits: One researcher read and coded transcripts and field notes against an a priori scheme. Observer bias possible.
agent_relevance: Real teams skip behaviour specification when goals are fuzzy. Our expected-behaviour stage must produce testable statements or it will be hollow.

source: Sahadevan et al. (2024) Automated extraction and creation of FBS design reasoning knowledge graphs from structured data in product catalogues lacking contextual information
finding: Rule-based plus NLP pipeline to turn spec sheets into FBS knowledge graphs. Human FBS experts disagree on classifying variables as F, B or S. ChatGPT given the written rules classified key-value pairs.
numbers: Three FBS experts: accuracy 54%, 93%, 87%. ChatGPT with rules: about 78% first, 100% after rule refinement (small test). Final classifier on 31 variables: accuracy 71%; F precision 73, recall 100, F1 85 (n=11); B 57/57/57 (n=7); S 78/54/64 (n=13).
limits: Tiny test sets (31 items, one electrical-connector domain, one company). The 100% was on rules refined against that set, so likely overfitted. Authors say FBS definitions are ambiguous and rules may not transfer.
agent_relevance: FBS labels are hard even for experts (54% to 93%). Function is easy to tag, behaviour is hardest. An LLM tagger needs code-checked rules, and we should expect B/S confusion.

source: Elhambakhsh, Grandi, Ko (2025) A domain adaptation of large language models for classifying mechanical assembly components
finding: Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 Turbo to label the function of mechanical parts (FBS function modelling). Un-tuned GPT models did poorly on the function class task.
numbers: OSDR 7568 parts; matched ABC set 6786 parts. Pre-trained test accuracy: GPT-3.5 Turbo 0.04, GPT-4 Turbo 0.27, GPT-4o Mini 0.20. Fine-tuned model test accuracy about 0.89 with only 10% (681 samples) of training data, falling to about 0.55-0.64 as the training share rose to 75-90%. On ABC, 99% of outputs fell inside the predefined classes.
limits: Accuracy fell with more training data; authors suggest overfitting; text and table numbers are not fully consistent. Class imbalance (channel and support dominate). Fixed label set limits new function classes. No human baseline.
agent_relevance: Zero-shot LLMs are poor at function labelling in engineering (4-27%). Do not trust a model's own F/B/S tags without a check; label sets must be closed and tested.

source: Fujiu et al. (2025) FBS model-based maintenance record accumulation for failure-cause inference in manufacturing systems
finding: FBS knowledge graph used to organise maintenance records for retrieval of failure causes (LEGO-car assembly line). FBS structure helped most in hard cases with few related records and differing vocabulary.
numbers: Graph: 165 nodes, 220 edges, plus 1176 record nodes. Hard case (Assumed Failure 2) at n=8: FBS method Precision 1.0, Recall 0.625; baseline Precision 0.50, Recall 0.375. Easy case (Failure 1): methods about equal; at n=35 precision slightly lower, recall higher.
limits: One small lab line, two assumed failures, one inference engine not tuned for the graph. Authors say precision fell where subgraphs were embedded as single chunks. Preprint.
agent_relevance: FBS hierarchy lets search be restricted to the same level. Useful as a retrieval index for hardware-debug style tasks, but evidence is thin.

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2023) Conceptual design generation using large language models (IDETC)
finding: GPT-3 solutions for 12 design problems vs crowdsourced solutions. Not FBS-specific, but the core computational concept-generation baseline. LLM solutions rated more feasible and useful; crowd solutions more novel. Few-shot prompting made outputs more like the crowd.
numbers: 600 solutions rated by 2 expert raters (kappa fair to moderate; 20 per prompt per mode, 120 double-rated); one-way ANOVA. Embedding cosine similarity of GPT-3 sets to crowd set: few-shot 0.804 (SD 0.06), zero-shot with 'unique' 0.746 (SD 0.06), base mean 0.748. GPT-3 repeats itself semantically over 100 outputs.
limits: GPT-3 era; 2 raters; similarity depends strongly on the prompt ID. Not a test of FBS.
agent_relevance: Typical LLM weakness in design: feasible but less novel, and repeating itself. G4 applies: many samples from one model are not independent.

source: Chen, Zuo, Cai, Yin, Zhang, Sun, Childs, Wang (2024) Toward controllable generative design: a conceptual design generation approach leveraging the function-behavior-structure ontology and large language models (J. Mech. Design 146(12), doi:10.1115/1.4065562)
finding: LLM infers FBS in three prompted sub-tasks (functional, behavioural, structural reasoning) with templates and specification signifiers. A human picks among generated function-structure pairs. In a comparative experiment it scored highest, with concepts judged more novel, useful, functional and low-cost than the baseline.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures obtained (full-text download returned HTTP 405).
quote: our approach achieves the highest scores in concept evaluation
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract and catalogue record. Sample size, model version and statistics unknown. Authors' own comparison, no independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Most direct FBS-as-prompt-scaffold study found. Decomposing a design prompt into F then B then S is the closest published analogue of our state chain; its effect size is unknown, so treat as untested.

source: Joshi et al. (2025) Leveraging large language models for enabling design by analogy: a computational framework (ICED25, Proc. Design Society 5:2251-2260)
finding: Conceptual pipeline: encode a problem as a dependency graph in FBS, cluster into abstract functions, retrieve analogues by embedding similarity with threshold tau, transfer structures in topological order, evaluate with FBS metrics, store in a vector database.
numbers: No experiment, no N, no metrics. One qualitative motorcycle case. Five phases: retrieval, mapping, transfer, evaluation, storage.
limits: Theory paper; claims about scale and efficiency are untested. Authors list empirical validation as future work.
agent_relevance: Shows the design-by-analogy pattern (function abstraction, retrieve, transfer) but offers no evidence for it. Do not borrow numbers from it.

source: Tanaka, Nomaguchi, Fujita (2026) Design ideation through LLM-driven design operation: a case study of architectural design using pattern language (Design Science 12:e23)
finding: Structured tree-of-thought design prompt (3 contexts, 3 functions each, 3 attributes each, pick top 10) with pattern language. FBS only cited as related work. It raised attribute diversity vs chain-of-thought but did not improve human creativity ratings.
numbers: gpt-4.1, temp 0, 100 runs per prompt per problem, 4 prompts x 3 problems, 400 alternatives; 8 expert raters on 2 alternatives per prompt/problem. Diversity (DPP) e.g. front porch: A 83.1, B 68.8, C 122.3, D 96.4. Mean human novelty 2.44-3.38; Prompt D rarely top. ICC values from -0.52 to 0.72.
limits: Very small human rating set (8 designs per problem); inter-rater agreement mostly low. Diversity metric gains did not carry over to rated quality.
agent_relevance: Structuring the model's function-to-attribute exploration widens embedding diversity, but humans did not rate the results higher. Diversity metrics alone should not be our success signal.

source: Wang et al. (2023) FBS-based stage-specific prompts with GPT-3 (as cited by Tanaka et al. 2026)
finding: Earlier use of GPT-3 with FBS-based stage-specific prompts, cited only in related work. Details not seen.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Known only from a citation; original not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Confirms that FBS-staged prompting has been tried since 2023; effect unknown.

source: Dorst & Cross (2001) and Maher & Poon (1996) via Gero & Milovanovic (2020): co-evolution of problem and solution
finding: Co-evolution accounts: designers alternate between exploring the problem space and the solution space, each updating the other. FBS issues can be regrouped into the two spaces to track this.
numbers: No numbers obtained; originals not opened.
limits: Known from a secondary review only. Maher & Poon's computational model of co-evolution was not read.
agent_relevance: Same alternation our schema allows via reframing; keep a problem-side revision path open (see Ralph, a17).
